title: Blog 1
content:
AMAZON ECS GATEWAY: A FULLY-MANAGED INGRESS SOLUTION FOR CONTAINER SERVICES Amazon ECS recently introduced Amazon ECS Gateway, an account-level resource that simplifies the entire ingress networking layer for containerized applications. This feature automatically provisions, configures, and manages the lifecycle of Application Load Balancers (ALBs), ACM certificates, DNS hostnames, and Security Groups directly inside your AWS account—eliminating the manual bottleneck of setting up ingress infrastructure separately for each microservice.
Key points to know:
Clear separation of responsibilities: Platform teams define centralized networking standards (Subnets, Security Groups, AWS WAF web ACLs, TLS certificates) in one place; application teams simply attach a gateway connector parameter to their service definition without needing deep networking expertise. Cost optimization through ALB sharing: Supports host-based routing, allowing up to 25 ECS services to share a single Application Load Balancer. Dynamic resource provisioning on demand: ECS automatically creates the first ALB when a service connects, scales out additional ALBs as capacity thresholds are reached, and deprovisions unused ALBs when no services remain attached. Instant ready-to-use endpoints: Every connected service receives a unique DNS hostname and matching ACM certificate automatically, ready to accept traffic as soon as deployment finishes. Flexible Many-to-Many connectivity: One Gateway can associate with up to 10,000 ECS clusters, and each ECS cluster can attach up to 5 Gateways (for example, separating internal VPC gateways from internet-facing gateways). Broad support and smooth adoption: Available for awsvpc networking across EC2, AWS Fargate, and ECS Managed Instances. Existing services with dedicated load balancers can attach a gateway connector for parallel testing before retiring old load balancers. This feature is especially valuable for organizations operating large-scale microservices architectures on ECS, helping accelerate release velocity while preventing network configuration drift across development teams.

title: Event 1

Connect participants through ice-breaking activities to share backgrounds and form teammates ahead of the challenge. Key Takeaways Design Mindset Build Real Products: Knowledge of Cloud and AI only creates real value when applied to build working solutions for concrete problems. Aligning AI with Business Context: Understanding business needs before deciding between prompting, RAG, or full Agentic AI workflows. Technical Architecture Understanding how Prompt Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Knowledge Bases, and AI Agents fit together inside a Generative AI application. Seeing the practical workflow for turning an idea into an AWS-backed prototype within a short hands-on timeframe. Selecting appropriate technical scope that aligns with real-world usability and Buildathon judging criteria. Application Strategy Approach the Buildathon systematically: verify problem value and judging criteria before adding unnecessary technical complexity. Leverage mentor feedback and community learning materials proactively to troubleshoot bottlenecks faster during prototyping. Applying to Work Preparing Architecture for Internship & Buildathon Projects: Combine AWS infrastructure with Agentic AI patterns to design practical, demonstrable prototypes. Practicing RAG & Prompt Engineering: Experiment with structured prompts and Knowledge Bases to improve response accuracy on domain-specific datasets. Planning AWS Learning & Certifications: Balance daily hands-on labs with structured AWS certification preparation following speaker advice. Learning from experienced speakers and mentors Heard candid, relatable career insights from Thien Lu (Program Manager, FCAJ), Truong Bui (Tech Lead, CMC Global), and Phong Pham (Program Manager, FCAJ) on how enterprises apply Cloud and Agentic AI. Received practical answers during the Q&A session regarding AWS certifications, real project readiness, and Buildathon strategy. Timely support from mentors helped clarify how the pieces connect end-to-end inside a limited session. Community networking and team building The lively Ice-breaking activity on the 26th floor of Bitexco helped me meet peers who share interests in Cloud and AI and connect with potential teammates. Closing Remarks wrapped up the morning with learning resources and memorable group photos alongside the AWS First Cloud AI Journey and CMC Global community. Lessons learned Growing in Cloud & AI requires combining solid technical fundamentals, hands-on product building, and effective teamwork. Asking speakers and mentors specific questions early is one of the fastest ways to clear both technical doubts and career direction questions. content:

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS LAMBDA WEB FUNCTIONS: RUN SERVERLESS HTTP WEB APPS DIRECTLY AWS recently introduced AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new serverless compute model that allows standard HTTP web applications and backend APIs to run directly on AWS Lambda without rewriting code into traditional event handlers or relying on adapter layers. Alongside this launch, traditional event-driven Lambda functions are renamed Lambda Event Functions (a naming distinction only, requiring zero changes to existing workloads), allowing developers to keep a familiar web-server development experience on serverless infrastructure.
Key points to know:
Native support for popular web frameworks: Code runs as a standard web server listening directly on an HTTP port (launching with the Node.js 24 runtime on Arm64 architecture), allowing immediate use of Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or React Router without wrapper libraries or complex translation layers. Concurrent request handling and reduced cold starts: Unlike the single-request event execution model, a warm Web Function execution environment (provisioned with 2 vCPUs and 2 GB of memory at launch) can process multiple HTTP requests concurrently, significantly reducing cold starts. Cost efficiency with Active Compute billing: Instead of paying for idle I/O wait time (such as waiting on database queries or downstream API calls), you are billed only for actual active CPU processing time, separated from memory and request charges. Native HTTP streaming support: Enables streaming partial responses to clients as soon as chunks are ready rather than buffering the entire payload—ideal for real-time interfaces and Generative AI workloads. Clear three-part resource model: Structured around Web Function (core resource holding name and settings), Revision (immutable snapshot of code and configuration enabling fast rollbacks), and Endpoint (network entry point providing a unique public HTTPS domain, authentication settings, and traffic routing rules). Multi-Region routing and Amazon VPC integration: Supports deploying once across multiple AWS Regions to automatically route traffic to the Region closest to users for lower latency, while integrating natively with Amazon VPC to communicate securely with databases and internal resources. This capability is particularly well suited for teams building modern web applications and backend APIs who want the simplicity of standard web frameworks alongside AWS Lambda’s automatic scaling, zero server management, and active-compute pricing model.

title: Create an S3 Interface endpoint
content:
In this section you will create and test an S3 interface endpoint using the simulated on-premises environment deployed as part of this workshop.
Return to the Amazon VPC menu. In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint.
In Create endpoint console:
Name the interface endpoint In Service category, choose aws services In the Search box, type S3 and press Enter. Select the endpoint named com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3. Ensure that the Type column indicates Interface. For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. Make sure to choose “VPC Cloud” and not “VPC On-prem”
Expand Additional settings and ensure that Enable DNS name is not selected (we will use this in the next part of the workshop) Select 2 subnets in the following AZs: us-east-1a and us-east-1b For Security group, choose SGforS3Endpoint: Keep the default policy - full access and click Create endpoint Congratulation on successfully creating S3 interface endpoint. In the next step, we will test the interface endpoint.

title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.

title: Blog 3
content:
AWS ACCOUNT ACCESS MANAGER: CENTRALIZED WORKFORCE ACCESS WITH IAM ROLE FLEXIBILITY AWS recently announced AWS Account Access Manager (AAM), a new AWS IAM capability that bridges centralized workforce access administration in AWS IAM Identity Center with the granular flexibility of local IAM roles inside individual AWS accounts. It eliminates the long-standing trade-off between centralized Permission Sets (which can be rigid to customize per account) and manually maintaining custom federation setups, enabling organizations to govern multi-account access consistently at scale.
Key points to know:
Direct IAM Role mapping from a centralized directory: Integrates with an organization instance of AWS IAM Identity Center (synced with users and groups from corporate IdPs such as Okta, Ping Identity, Cisco Duo, or Microsoft Entra ID), allowing administrators to assign existing account-level IAM roles to users and groups from a single management view. Preserves full native IAM Role capabilities: Retains all native IAM role features including custom trust policies, role paths, attribute-based access control (ABAC), and IAM role tags for cost allocation. Autonomy for builders with centralized governance: Application and workload teams remain free to author and tune IAM roles to fit project-specific requirements, while security and platform teams maintain central visibility and control across the entire AWS Organization. User-level audit attribution and multi-channel sign-in: Uses trusted identity propagation to carry individual user context into assumed role sessions, ensuring AWS CloudTrail logs pinpoint the exact human identity behind every action rather than just a generic role name; supports login via Account Access Portal, AWS Access Portal, or AWS CLI (aws login). Coexists smoothly with Permission Sets: No big-bang migration is required—organizations can use Account Access Manager in accounts that need specialized IAM role configurations while keeping existing Permission Sets elsewhere. IaC automation at no extra charge: Supports provisioning and scaling via AWS CloudFormation, AWS CLI, Terraform, and Pulumi, and is available at no additional cost (you only pay for underlying AWS resources) across AWS Commercial Regions. This feature is especially useful for multi-account AWS environments where security teams need centralized governance and user-level auditing without slowing down engineering teams configuring fine-grained application permissions.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.

Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS. title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Here, you can freely share your personal opinions about your experience participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program. This will help the FCAJ team improve any shortcomings based on the following aspects:
Overall Evaluation 1. Working Environment
The learning and event space at the Bitexco office is comfortable, tidy, and welcoming. Everyone in the FCAJ community is approachable and willing to discuss or point out troubleshooting directions when I get stuck on a lab or configuration detail. However, since most participants complete weekly labs remotely at their own pace, adding a few small-group meetups or casual catch-ups would make it even easier to connect with peers.
2. Support from Mentor / Team Admin
Mentors and the admin team were supportive from onboarding and administrative setup through the offline events. What worked well for me is that when I asked questions, mentors usually pointed me toward checking the relevant logs or documentation rather than handing over the answer immediately, which helped me retain the knowledge and fix similar issues myself later on.
3. Relevance of Work to Academic Major
My university major is Artificial Intelligence (AI), so the first few weeks covering VPC networking, routing, and IAM permissions felt unfamiliar at first. However, once the track moved into data pipelines, serverless workflows, and services like Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker, it became very clear how closely cloud infrastructure supports deploying AI systems in practice.
4. Learning & Skill Development Opportunities
Over the 12 weeks, besides getting hands-on practice with services across the AWS Console and CLI, I built better habits in reading English technical docs, maintaining consistent weekly worklogs, and keeping track of resource cleanup to avoid unexpected charges. Attending talkshows and mini challenges at offline events also gave me a clearer sense of how companies apply Cloud and AI in production.
5. Company Culture & Team Spirit
The overall atmosphere is positive and respectful. During offline sessions like the Buildrathon Kickoff and Watch Party at the AWS office, attendees interacted naturally, found teammates quickly, and helped each other work through hands-on challenges even when meeting for the first time.
6. Internship Policies / Benefits
The program offers helpful schedule flexibility, making it manageable for students balancing internship tasks alongside university classes and coursework projects. Having access to the structured AWS Study Group curriculum along with invitations to in-person events at the AWS office was a major highlight.
Additional Questions What did you find most satisfying during your internship?
What satisfied me most was having a clear, step-by-step AWS hands-on curriculum from basics to advanced topics, combined with in-person events at the AWS Vietnam office. That combination made cloud infrastructure much less intimidating and gave me confidence to explore areas like Agentic AI and Serverless. What do you think the company should improve for future interns?
The team could consider hosting short periodic technical review or Q&A sessions in small groups (online or offline) so newer participants can troubleshoot configuration issues together faster instead of getting stuck alone for too long. If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they intern here? Why or why not?
Yes, especially for students who want a solid foundation in AWS or want to explore combining Cloud and AI. The lab path is structured, documentation is accessible in both Vietnamese and English, and the FCAJ community is supportive. Suggestions & Expectations Do you have any suggestions to improve the internship experience?
Including a quick-reference checklist early in the program highlighting resources that are easiest to forget and incur Free Tier charges (beyond standard cleanup steps) would give newcomers extra peace of mind while experimenting. Would you like to continue this program in the future?
Yes, I would gladly participate in future FCAJ community workshops or help support upcoming cohorts if the opportunity arises. Any other comments (free sharing):
Thank you to the FCAJ team, mentors, and admins for supporting me throughout the three-month internship. It has been a very practical learning period before taking on larger projects ahead.
